title: Finite products of abelian categories with enough injectives
statement: Let $I$ be a finite set and let $(\mathcal A_i)_{i\in I}$ be abelian categories [def-sp-abelian], each with enough injectives [def-sp-injective-resolutions]. Their product category $\prod_{i\in I}\mathcal A_i$ is abelian, has enough injectives, and an object $(J_i)_i$ is injective exactly when every $J_i$ is injective in $\mathcal A_i$. For any family of objects $(A_i)_i$, a componentwise choice of injective resolutions $A_i\to J_i^\bullet$ is an injective resolution of $(A_i)_i$ in the product category.

source.place: Homological Algebra / Derived Categories, Section 0156 (derived-section-right-derived-functor, derived.tex line 6939): right derived functors computed from injective resolutions; product-category formulation supplied by the worker

proof.text: Form the product category with objects $(A_i)_{i\in I}$ and componentwise morphisms. The zero object, finite biproducts, kernels, and cokernels are obtained componentwise. A componentwise morphism is a monomorphism (respectively epimorphism) exactly when every component is, and the componentwise kernel (respectively cokernel) has the universal property. Thus the kernel-of-monomorphism and cokernel-of-epimorphism conditions hold componentwise; together with preadditivity, zero object, and biproducts this makes the product category abelian by [def-sp-abelian].

source.place: componentwise check against the definition of an abelian category (no Stacks statement for product categories)

proof.text: Let $J=(J_i)_i$. By Step 1, kernels in the product category are computed componentwise, so a morphism $M\to N$ of the product category is a monomorphism exactly when every component $M_i\to N_i$ is. Since $\operatorname{Hom}(N,J)=\prod_i\operatorname{Hom}(N_i,J_i)$ and $\operatorname{Hom}(M,J)=\prod_i\operatorname{Hom}(M_i,J_i)$, the restriction map $\operatorname{Hom}(N,J)\to\operatorname{Hom}(M,J)$ is the product of the componentwise restriction maps. If every $J_i$ is injective, each componentwise restriction is surjective [def-sp-injective-resolutions], hence so is their product, and $J$ is injective. Conversely, suppose $J$ is injective and let $M_i\hookrightarrow N_i$ be a monomorphism and $M_i\to J_i$ a map in $\mathcal A_i$. Place them in the $i$-th component with zero objects and zero maps in the other components; the result is a monomorphism and a map into $J$ in the product category, which extends along the monomorphism; its $i$-th component is the required extension $N_i\to J_i$. Hence $J$ is injective exactly when every $J_i$ is.

source.place: componentwise check against the definition of an injective object; cf. Lemma Tag 0137 (lemma-product-injectives) for the analogous statement inside one category

proof.text: For each $A_i$, choose a monomorphism $A_i\hookrightarrow J_i$ with $J_i$ injective, using the enough-injectives hypothesis. Their componentwise product is a monomorphism in the product category, and its target is injective by the preceding componentwise characterization. Therefore the product category has enough injectives.

source.place: Injective resolutions setup preceding Lemma Tag 0137; componentwise construction supplied here

proof.text: Choose injective resolutions $A_i\to J_i^\bullet$ in the component categories. The componentwise maps give a morphism $(A_i)_i\to (J_i^\bullet)_i$ of cochain complexes. Every term is injective by the componentwise characterization. Kernels and images of each differential are computed componentwise, so the complex is exact in every nonzero degree precisely when each $J_i^\bullet$ is; its degree-zero cohomology is $(A_i)_i$. Thus the componentwise complex is an injective resolution in the product category, by the definition [def-sp-injective-resolutions].
